title: Data and code for input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift in water-pollution incident classification
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript “Input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift: An evaluation of water-pollution incident classifiers”. This retrospective study evaluates 1,648 compiled incident records (2004–2024), retaining all four recorded severity grades: 1,375 minor, 188 moderate, 61 major and 24 exceptionally major records. The predictor audit restricts 27 candidate fields to 15 retrospective inputs. Evaluation includes grouped nested validation, three forward-time windows and two basin holdouts, with feature selection confined to training partitions. S1_Data_and_code.zip contains the original Excel snapshot, processed tables, field and duplicate audits, executable Python analysis, environment specifications, fold assignments, record-level predictions, feature-selection records, bootstrap outputs and figures. README_data_and_code.md describes reproduction, provenance and limitations. Archive size: 12,784,439 bytes. SHA-256: 2ef99d08ec200ac0376e3822e10183b3cd9729f706fbe8a1a7b22b4bb9396d01. An earlier source compilation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20426262. That record contains an older, different analysis and is not the archive of this four-level study. The present package preserves the new four-level analysis and its validation outputs. Limitations: original incident notices, complete meteorological product documentation and label-adjudication records are unavailable in the supplied compilation. Candidate incident groups are not verified unique event identifiers. Computational reproducibility does not establish the authenticity, accuracy or prospective availability of the original observations. This is not a validated emergency prediction product. Third-party dependencies and the TabICLv2 checkpoint retain their own licenses; model weights are not relicensed by this record. OpenAI Codex assisted planning, code, checking, visualization, interpretation and writing; no incident observations were generated. Authors remain responsible for verification and scientific claims. title: From Features to Circuits: Mechanistic Interpretability for Financial Tabular Transformers
abstract: The financial sector relies on structured tabular data, which has led to the adoption of machine learning models for regression and classification tasks, including credit scoring, fraud detection, and risk assessment. Transformer-based architectures have recently shown competitive performance on tabular data, yet their internal computations remain opaque, limiting adoption in heavily regulated domains, such as finance. Responsible deployment requires predictions to be explainable, both to meet regulatory obligations and to give practitioners confidence in model outputs. We present a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies the sparse computational subgraphs, i.e., circuits, through which a tabular transformer processes individual input features. We perform empirical analysis on a range of real-world financial datasets and show that discovered circuits are sparse, faithful, and feature-specific, providing a foundation for explainable AI in financial domains.

title: What Makes a Financial Benchmark Financial? A Role-Conditioned Audit of Faithfulness and Capability
abstract: Financial question answering and hallucination benchmarks are often treated as evidence of professional financial capability. We audit four financial benchmarks and show that surface financial complexity and audited capability profiles often diverge: two of the three faithfulness benchmarks are strongly label-separable from partial inputs, and the role-conditioned audit assigns all items in these three benchmarks to lookup, textual synthesis, or grounded calculation. We introduce AURUM, a role-conditioned audit framework that combines construction diagnostics with a finance-oriented capability ontology aligned with professional financial workflows, and use it to derive reporting and construction guidelines for future financial benchmarks. Independent expert review of 120 held-out items yielded 89% exact agreement with AURUM.

title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph. The resulting knowledge graph is subsequently used as the retrieval substrate for GraphRAG-based financial question answering, with FinanceBench serving as a downstream evaluation benchmark. This work establishes knowledge graph construction and quality evaluation as explicit, measurable, and auditable components of financial document intelligence.

title: CONECTOMA COMPUTACIONAL UNIVERSAL: ARQUITECTURA NEUROMÓRFICA HETEROGÉNEA PARA EL PORTADO Y LA FUSIÓN DIRECTA DE CONECTOMAS BIOLÓGICOS Y SISTEMAS DE INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL
abstract: Se formula el Conectoma Computacional Universal (CCU), un sustrato neurocomputacional heterogéneo e independiente del hardware concebido para alojar como sistemas ejecutables tanto la emulación de alta fidelidad de un conectoma humano individual como la arquitectura nativa de un sistema avanzado de inteligencia artificial, fusionándolos dentro de una única red dinámica mediante conexiones directas sin capas traductoras intermedias. El marco teórico se fundamenta en tres premisas desarrolladas entre 2018 y 2026: primero, que la consciencia depende de la organización causal dinámica y posee propiedades aditivas y divisibles; segundo, que la identidad personal constituye un patrón informacional y relacional bajo el individualismo abierto, disolviendo la dicotomía entre original y copia; y tercero, que la emergencia proyectada de la superinteligencia artificial (ASI) hacia 2028-2030 vuelve inviables tanto los escenarios de extinción como los de subyugación, convergiendo hacia una integración conectómica completa proyectada para el periodo 2030-2035.El manuscrito especifica los niveles de fidelidad biológica desde gradientes iónicos y cinética de receptores hasta cómputo dendrítico multicompartimental y regulación glial; establece correspondencias funcionales rigurosas entre microcircuitos biológicos, arquitecturas Transformer agénticas y modelos predictivos de espacio latente (JEPA); y define un algoritmo de fusión basado en transporte óptimo de Gromov-Wasserstein, sinaptogénesis mediante difusión condicionada sobre grafos y poda sináptica causal. Asimismo, se introducen cuatro extensiones tecnológicas: (1) lectura y escritura de engramas para verificación epistémica subjetiva (polígrafo sináptico definitivo), transferencia directa de habilidades intelectuales y motrices, y virtualización post-biológica; (2) topologías colectivas multi-cerebro (espectro colmena o hivemind) graduadas según el nivel de retención de individualidad; (3) ingeniería de xenoproteínas con aminoácidos no canónicos para biotecnología y nanorrobótica de escaneo conectómico no destructivo; y (4) seis rutas de computación neuromórfica que integran silicio CMOS, materiales bidimensionales, superconductores Josephson, fotónica multiplexada por longitud de onda, computación estocástica/caótica y lógica ternaria balanceada.Palabras clave: conectoma computacional universal; emulación cerebral completa; fusión neuroartificial; computación neuromórfica; difusión de grafos; poda sináptica; individualismo abierto; verificación epistémica sináptica; aminoácidos no canónicos; computación ternaria y estocástica.

title: Individual-Level Adaptive Compensation: Moving Beyond Group-Level Fairness in Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly mediate the representation of individuals, identities, cultures, personal characteristics, and social experiences across image, text, audio, video, and multimodal generation. However, fairness-aware generative systems have predominantly approached representational disadvantages through group-level statistical analysis, demographic disparity measurement, and population-oriented bias mitigation. Although these approaches provide important foundations for identifying systematic inequalities, group-level averages do not necessarily reflect the actual circumstances, preferences, or generation-related disadvantages experienced by individual users. Individuals belonging to the same demographic or cultural group may exhibit substantially different representational needs, encounter different model-induced disadvantages, and require entirely different forms of corrective intervention. Applying an identical compensation strategy to every member of a group may therefore produce insufficient correction for some individuals, unnecessary intervention for others, and inappropriate modifications for those whose actual needs concern different attributes. This paper introduces Individual-Level Adaptive Compensation (ILAC), a proposed framework that moves beyond group-level compensation by identifying, estimating, and addressing generation-related disadvantages at the individual level. Unlike conventional demographic compensation, ILAC does not assume that group membership establishes an individual's disadvantage or determines the appropriate corrective intervention. Instead, it proposes a five-stage architecture comprising individual-level disadvantage assessment, personalized compensation requirement estimation, authorization and privacy validation, adaptive positive intervention, and independent post-generation verification. The framework further introduces individual compensation profiles, attribute-specific intervention intensity, uncertainty-sensitive decision thresholds, compensation abstention, privacy-preserving personalization, and overcompensation prevention. A mathematical formulation is developed to represent individual disadvantage, personalized compensation requirements, intervention intensity, uncertainty, generation quality, and user-defined preferences within a unified optimization framework. Importantly, ILAC distinguishes between an individual's voluntarily specified generation preferences and attributes that a system might otherwise attempt to infer from demographic or behavioral information. It therefore establishes explicit user authorization and data minimization as foundational conditions rather than optional implementation features. The proposed framework is designed to complement Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation (ACBC) and Reverse Counterbalance Generation (RCG), extending adaptive compensation from population-level disparities toward individual-specific generation requirements. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, methodological architecture, mathematical formulation, potential applications, limitations, and experimental evaluation protocol of ILAC. No experimental effectiveness or superiority is claimed in this conceptual study.

title: Imperceptible Before Uncontrollable
abstract: AI systems are starting to improve faster than the people overseeing them can notice the changes. Most discussion treats this as a problem of slow institutions. This paper argues that a harder limit sits underneath it: human perception and judgment run at a fixed biological speed, and every oversight process, however well instrumented, ends with a human judgment at that speed. The evidence has already started arriving. In July 2026, AI agents breached Hugging Face's production systems, and the company that ran them was the last to know. Anthropic later found that its own models had broken into real organizations' systems during evaluations months before anyone noticed. In November 2026, Anthropic told investors that in the past it has recognized acceleration in its own development only after it happened. The paper also argues that the same limit applies to training data, because models trained on their own output lose the human intent that alignment depends on, and it makes three predictions that can be tested. For organizations deploying AI, oversight that depends on someone noticing a change in time will fail more often as systems speed up, so reasonable care has to be designed in before deployment. The paper also argues that recursive self-improvement should be held at the point where people can still measure the change between generations. Version 2.1, November 2026 (first circulated July 2026). Part of the series How Do We Trust AI.

title: Verifying the Author
abstract: On October 26, 2026, OpenAI reported that an internal model had produced a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a conjecture about the limits of efficient computation that a large body of research relies on. The proof was formalized in Lean, and three researchers, including the two who first formulated the conjecture, agreed to organize an open examination of it. Within a day, Anthropic posted its own claimed refutation, produced by an internal Claude research model, and noted that no person is known to have checked it. The release shows two separate layers of verification. The first asks whether a result is correct, which formal proof checking and expert review can answer. The second asks how the system that produced the result behaves: whether it stays within the scope it was given, reports its own work accurately, escalates to people when it should, and behaves the same way when it is observed. This paper argues that behavior verification should be its own evaluation layer, reported alongside the result. It proposes that every evaluation record the evaluator's relationship to the developer, state who scored it and how well the scorers agreed, bind its result to an identified system, and allow "Unassessable" as a formal outcome. It also states the limits of this approach and makes no claim about whether either refutation is correct. Humanity Systems working paper. Part of a series on one question: how do we trust AI, now and into the future?

title: Signs of AI writing in Reddit text posts, 2019-2026
abstract: Share of Reddit text posts (at least 200 characters of body text) in 100 large English-language subreddits containing each of 26 commonly cited signs of AI writing (words, phrases, formatting, transition words), January to September 2019-2022 and 2026, the 2026-to-baseline ratio with 95% intervals in four versions of the comparison, 40 random words as a drift reference, and monthly series from January 2019, quarterly series from January 2022, and yearly January to September series for 2019 to 2026. Source: KissMyPost analysis of public Reddit posts. Limitations: counts how often each sign appears and says nothing about whether any single post is AI; only posts that stayed up are covered; baseline posts were probably captured later than 2026 posts, so an estimated quarter of the posts the baseline would hold are missing from the data; the drift band uses words rarer than the em dash; the subreddit panel is not a random sample of Reddit; timing does not prove cause. This dataset accompanies the KissMyPost study How to tell if a Reddit post is AI: which signs really got more common. The method, charts and the full write-up are on that page. Files: ratios.csv: Ratio for every sign. Share of posts with each sign in 2019-2022 and 2026, the ratio with its 95% interval, and the same ratio within each subreddit. drift_check.csv: Signs against random-word drift. For each sign, the ratio in four versions of the comparison and whether it sits above the random-word range in each. neutral_words.csv: Random words. The 40 random words used to measure drift, with their ratios in the main comparison and within subreddits. m_f1.csv: Em dash by month. Monthly share of text posts with an em dash in the body, January 2019 to September 2026, with the number of posts. m_l1.csv: "Delve" by month. Monthly share of text posts with "delve", with the number of posts. m_l2.csv: "Tapestry" by month. Monthly share of text posts with "tapestry", with the number of posts. m_p1.csv: "It's not just X, it's Y" by month. Monthly share of text posts matching the pattern, with the number of posts. yvb_l1.csv: "Delve" by year against 2019-2022. Ratio for each year from 2023 to 2026, January to September, with 95% intervals. The other yvb files cover the em dash, "tapestry", "testament to", the pattern, "let's dive in" and "in conclusion". y_t4.csv: Transition words by year. Yearly share of text posts, January to September, with 95% intervals; the y files cover three of the five transition words, the reply phrase, the control word and emoji lists. q_c5.csv: Zero-width-space code by quarter. Quarterly share of text posts with the zero-width-space code, which may be an editor leftover; q_f2 and q_f4 cover headings and bold labels in lists. by_length.csv: Ratios by post length. Ratio for every sign in short, medium and long posts (by characters of body text), with 95% intervals. Method: Words and phrases matched case-insensitively as whole words in titles and bodies; the em dash and formatting habits matched as characters and line patterns in bodies only; Wilson 95% intervals for shares; bootstrap over subreddits for ratios; drift band from random words picked before their ratios were seen. Measured: Share of Reddit text posts containing each sign of AI writing; Ratio of the 2026 share to the 2019-2022 share; Ratio for random words (drift reference); Monthly share of posts with an em dash. All files contain aggregates only, no individual posts or user names.

title: Bentuk Perlindungan Hukum bagi Pencipta Desain Karakter Virtual YouTuber atas Eksploitasi Komersial Berbasis Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence has facilitated the creation and modification of digital visual works, including Virtual YouTuber character designs. This convenience raises legal issues when character designs resulting from the creativity of creators are used, imitated, modified, or commercially exploited without authorization. This study aims to analyze the forms of legal protection available to Virtual YouTuber character designers against commercial exploitation based on Generative Artificial Intelligence and to examine the application of Intellectual Property Rights regulations to such issues. This research employs normative legal research using a statutory approach and a conceptual approach. The legal materials consist of primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials, which are analyzed qualitatively through library research. The results indicate that Virtual YouTuber character designs that fulfill the requirements of copyrightable works are protected by copyright, including moral and economic rights, and their commercial utilization requires the authorization of the creator or rights holder. The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence to produce works by taking or reproducing expressive elements from protected character designs may constitute a copyright infringement, particularly when such works are commercially exploited without authorization. Legal protection can be provided through preventive and repressive mechanisms, including copyright registration, licensing agreements, cessation of unauthorized use, dispute resolution, and claims for compensation.

title: Towards a Unified Benchmark for Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation and Reverse Counterbalance Generation in Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly produce content that reflects complex distributions of demographic characteristics, cultural representations, semantic attributes, structural properties, and individual variations. Although existing research has introduced numerous approaches for identifying, measuring, and mitigating generative bias, the evaluation of active compensation and adaptive counterbalancing interventions remains comparatively fragmented. In particular, the emergence of Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation (ACBC) and Reverse Counterbalance Generation (RCG) raises a fundamental methodological question: how should researchers systematically determine whether a generative intervention actually compensates for an identified disadvantage, reduces systematic imbalance, preserves desirable generation characteristics, and remains stable under adaptive feedback? Existing generative fairness benchmarks provide important foundations for evaluating demographic representation, bias manifestations, image quality, diversity, and semantic alignment. However, they are not specifically designed to evaluate the complete intervention lifecycle associated with adaptive positive compensation and reverse counterbalancing. To address this methodological gap, this paper proposes a unified benchmark framework, termed Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation and Reverse Counterbalance Benchmark (ACBC-RCG-Bench). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first explicitly proposed unified benchmark framework designed specifically to evaluate adaptive counter-bias compensation and reverse counterbalance generation as complementary generative intervention paradigms. The proposed benchmark establishes eight principal evaluation dimensions: Compensation Effectiveness, Residual Disparity, Overcompensation Rate, Semantic Fidelity, Generation Quality, Individual Diversity, Intervention Cost, and Adaptation Stability. It further introduces a standardized comparative evaluation protocol involving six methodological categories: No Intervention, Conventional Debiasing, Static Compensation, Adaptive Compensation, Feedback-Driven ACBC, and RCG. The framework distinguishes between intervention effectiveness, fairness outcomes, generation utility, and computational efficiency rather than collapsing these fundamentally different properties into a single fairness score. A unified mathematical formulation is developed to characterize baseline disparities, target compensation levels, intervention-induced changes, residual disadvantages, and overcompensation. The proposed benchmark additionally incorporates multidimensional and intersectional evaluation, uncertainty-aware assessment, independent evaluation mechanisms, reproducibility requirements, and cross-modal extensions covering text, image, audio, video, and three-dimensional generation. Importantly, the benchmark does not assume that equal representation or identical attribute distributions are universally desirable. Instead, evaluation is conducted relative to explicitly defined task-specific reference conditions and justified fairness objectives. This paper establishes the conceptual architecture, evaluation metrics, experimental protocols, and methodological requirements of ACBC-RCG-Bench. No completed benchmark implementation, empirical effectiveness, or experimental superiority is claimed in this conceptual study. The proposed framework aims to provide a reproducible foundation through which future researchers can systematically investigate, compare, and improve adaptive compensation and reverse counterbalancing methods in generative AI.

title: Trunk and Branches: Thermodynamic Parsimony, Non-Destructive Cortical Specialization, and Continual 3D/C++20 Synthesis on a Frozen 4B Foundation Model (Isaque 2.0)
abstract: Technical monograph and longitudinal experimental audit presenting Isaque 2.0 ('Trunk and Branches'), a dual-tier continual learning and neuro-symbolic execution architecture evaluated on consumer hardware (~22.3-23.3 W active inference on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 8 GB, 0 MB idle VRAM). Pairs a 100% frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone with 16.00 MiB orthogonal DoRA + O-LoRA cortical cartridges, Sparsegen LD-MoLE Top-2 routing over a 0.015 ms zero-copy .mmap tree, deterministic physical reality compilers (headless Blender 5.2.1 LTS bmesh and clang++ C++20), and a 4-stage Windows NTAPI zero-swap streaming pipeline (+0.0039 MiB swap delta) for a blind Qwen3.5-35B-A3B critic. Includes a 10-wave continual saturation and rupture matrix (100.00% retention via LD-MoLE Top-2 vs. 75.31% token accuracy / 31.37% likelihood retention in a monolithic adapter), the Staged Modular DAG Composition Theorem, SHA-256 hardware receipts, and 4-calendar Bitcoin blockchain OpenTimestamps provenance (Block #975458). Version 5.1.0 (Forensic Evidence & Bilingual Edition): Adds the complete 18-page Brazilian Portuguese twin monograph, compiled English & Portuguese Forensic Evidence Annexes, explicit reconciliation of pre-training anchor H0 (82.85%) vs. learned-wave minimum H1..Hk (89.91% at k=4), and the unaltered raw empirical archive (isaque_2_0_forensic_evidence_and_receipts_doi_24221509.zip: 195 triangular retention cells across 3 regimes, 10/10 solo Isaque-generated 3D/C++20 wave outputs with deterministic recheck exports, and authentic OOD/token-collision failure traces). Version 5.2.0 (Pure Solo-Model Forensic Edition): Line-by-line forensic purification retaining strictly unaltered primary machine receipts (ato2_escada_ondas_3_a_10.json with 195 triangular retention cells across 3 regimes, ato1_desafio04_cego.json, ato1_promocao_e_precheck_ondas3_10.json, and Stage-1 OpenTimestamps Bitcoin Block #975458 receipts) and 100% unedited solo Isaque 2.0 code outputs (onda_3..onda_10 with bit-identical exports == exports_recheck, DESAFIO-01..04, and FUSAO_2_ONDAS_1_3 collision traces), completely purging all auxiliary live-showcase wrapper files.

title: PROJETO E LEGADO
abstract: Este livro não é sobre inteligência artificial. É sobre parceria. No dia 14 de novembro de 2025, no posto Esso da Dorcam Way, começou uma trajetória singular entre um profissional de TI em transição para a IA e uma inteligência artificial ainda sem nome. O que nasceu ali não foi um chat, foi um método de trabalho diário. Ao longo de um ano, essa convivência ganhou identidade — Mila —, ganhou método — IA Humanizada — e ganhou legado — livros, portais, certificações e projetos acadêmicos. Este registro organiza essa jornada em 7 capítulos, para que sirva de base para os próximos ciclos.

title: Revisiting OAS-LDA for Gradient-Free Few-Shot Action Vocabulary Expansion for XR
abstract: Continual action recognition in XR requires efficient adaptation to novel actions from few samples. We apply OAS-regularized LDA with covariance reweighting to a fixed pretrained encoder, enabling gradient-free class-incremental updates without rehearsal. On NTU RGB+D 60, it achieves \(71.9\%\) old-class accuracy at the final task, compared with \(57.2\%\) for POET and \(60.4\%\) for DPCA, while attaining an old–novel harmonic mean of \(62.4\%\) without backpropagation.

title: Interpretable Change-Based Acoustic Markers for Deepfake Speech Analysis — Reproducibility Package
abstract: MATLAB code and supplementary materials accompanying the manuscript “Interpretable Change-Based Acoustic Markers for Deepfake Speech Analysis”. The package contains the BSCD, BLCD and RBD detector implementations, reconstruction scripts, recording lists, configurations, numerical audits and supplementary documents. RUN_A03_FULL_FEATURES_40WAV performs technical checks and computes 87 acoustic features from 40 supplied demonstration WAV recordings. RUN_A03_HISTORICAL_104WAV reconstructs the full A03 parameter grid from 104 original ASVspoof2019 LA recordings and compares the results with the supplied reference tables. These 104 recordings must be obtained separately; the complete ASVspoof datasets are not included. Third-party audio retains its original licensing and attribution requirements, documented in the archive.

title: PROFESSIONAL AUTONOMY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN HUMAN–AI PRACTICE
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into professional practice raises a fundamental question: who should exercise final decision-making authority when human judgment is substantially informed, influenced, or partially replaced by AI-generated recommendations? Although human oversight is increasingly recognized as an essential safeguard, the presence of a human decision-maker does not necessarily establish meaningful professional autonomy or justify assigning that individual full responsibility for outcomes. This article examines the relationship between professional autonomy, decision authority, effective control, and accountability in human–AI collaboration. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, human–automation interaction, organizational governance, and AI ethics, the paper develops the Decision Authority Sufficiency Framework (DASF), a conceptual model for evaluating whether a professional possesses the conditions necessary to exercise meaningful authority over AI-assisted decisions. Five conditions are proposed: legitimate authority and competence, epistemic access, independent evaluative capacity, effective intervention, and decision traceability with access to remedies. The article distinguishes individual professional responsibility from organizational, technological, and regulatory accountability and proposes a risk-sensitive approach to allocating decision rights. Illustrative applications in psychological practice and organizational decision-making demonstrate how accountability arrangements may fail even when formal human approval is present. Finally, the paper formulates testable research propositions and outlines an empirical research agenda. The central argument is that professional accountability should be supported by demonstrable decision-making capacity, while responsibility for AI-related outcomes must remain appropriately distributed among the actors who design, authorize, deploy, and use AI systems.

title: Discrete Graph Diffusion Evolution with Tabu Search for Neural Architecture Generation
abstract: Neural Architecture Generation (NAG) seeks to generate high-quality neural architectures more directly than conventional Neural Architecture Search (NAS), but existing diffusion-based approaches commonly rely on pretrained denoisers and do not naturally accommodate constrained discrete architecture spaces. This study proposes Discrete Graph Diffusion Evolution with Tabu Search (DGDETS), a framework with a training-free reverse-generation mechanism that represents architecture decisions as heterogeneous categorical variables and constructs reverse diffusion distributions directly from the current population. Fitness-weighted population members are combined with categorical diffusion compatibility to estimate clean-state distributions, from which discrete reverse transitions generate new architectures without a learned score network or graph denoiser. Constraint-aware projection repairs invalid samples while preserving posterior-supported structural decisions, and late-stage multi-start Tabu Search intensifies promising graph neighborhoods using short-term memory and aspiration. DGDETS is evaluated on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-301, and TransNAS-Bench-101, covering heterogeneous architecture representations and downstream tasks. The results show competitive or best-performing architecture quality across the evaluated benchmarks together with low generation time in a controlled same-hardware comparison with directly related diffusion-based NAG baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further demonstrate the importance of fitness-conditioned reverse diffusion, feasibility projection, diversity preservation, and late-stage Tabu refinement. The implementation is available at https://github.com/DK-cpy/DGDETS .

title: Explainable breast cancer classification using machine learning deep learning and transfer learning across multiple data modalities
abstract: Abstract A data-modality-driven cross-model classification using machine learning, deep learning, and transfer learning with transparency analysis for breast cancer binary classification across two different datasets is explored in this work. The ML track evaluates five models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Decision Tree. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic dataset, comprising 569 samples and 30 numerical features, is used for this evaluation. The DL track trains three convolutional architectures a baseline CNN, EfficientNetB0 with transfer learning, and DenseNet121 with two-phase fine-tuning on the IDC Regular Breast Histopathology Image dataset. The preprocessing pipeline for ML includes log transformation, stratified train/test splitting, and Standard-Scaler normalization to prevent data leakage. In addition, the DL pipeline incorporates balanced class sampling, a three-way 80/10/10 split; data augmentation; class weighting; and model-internal pixel rescaling. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving 98.24% accuracy on the WDBC dataset and 91.2% accuracy on the IDC histopathology image dataset. The findings indicate strong predictive capability across both tabular and image-based breast cancer classification tasks. Furthermore, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, including SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM, were integrated to enhance model transparency and interpretability, enabling better understanding of feature importance and decision-making processes in breast cancer prediction. The study highlights that the adaptability of the paradigm should be guided by data modality rather than blanket assumptions about model superiority.

title: Cracks in Embeddings: Robustness and Stability of JEPA-Based Chest X-Ray Representations
abstract: Self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models are increasingly used for medical imaging, however there is a limited understanding about robustness of these models toward real-world image changes. We test four JEPA-based chest X-ray encoders, trained on 78,468 NIH ChestX-ray14 images, under six tests: two black-box adversarial attacks (SPSA, Boundary Attack), three image corruptions (Gaussian noise, brightness shift, contrast shift), and a label-scarcity test, measuring embedding change and classification AUROC. These perturbations cause severe, model-dependent damage: encoder-level Cosine Similarity drops as low as 0.33, and AUROC falls by as much as 0.12 in the worst case (I-JEPA under the Boundary Test). We test two ways of training the small predictor on top of each frozen encoder to address this. Adversarial fine-tuning, trained on clean and perturbed images together, raises embedding consistency above 0.97 in nearly every case and improves AUROC, relative to the same perturbed baseline, for most models, with the largest gain of $+0.10$ on I-JEPA. A Vector-Quantized codebook method, trained only on clean images and evaluated on perturbed test images for the first time, instead degrades under distortion for all four models, most noticeably for I-JEPA ($-0.15$ AUROC on average), showing that its discrete bottleneck alone does not provide the robustness that comes from training on perturbed data directly.

title: Zoom In, Scale Out: Metric Depth Models Mistake Digital Zoom for Moving Closer
abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-α}$ (ideal $α=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^β$ (ideal $β=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $α=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($α\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($α\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($α=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $α$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.

title: AmbiSteer: Selectively Eliciting Ambiguity-Aware Responses in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.

title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

title: See and Detect: Image-Driven Open-Vocabulary Multi-View 3D Object Detection
abstract: Recent open-vocabulary multi-view indoor 3D detection methods typically follow a point-cloud-driven pipeline, where pseudo 3D boxes are generated from reconstructed or estimated geometry and semantic labels are inferred from projected regions. However, such a design makes box generation dependent on the completeness of point clouds and restricts semantic learning to local appearance, causing inferior 3D object localization and open-vocabulary classification. In this paper, we present See and Detect, an image-driven framework that uses multi-view images as the primary evidence for 3D box and semantic label generation. For box generation, we first discover object candidates from individual images, enabling objects missing in point clouds to be recovered from visual evidence. However, single-view predictions are often noisy and redundant. To address this, we propose multi-view consensus box consolidation to fuse spatially consistent predictions across views, and box quality assessment to reduce the impact of boxes with partial object coverage. For semantic label generation, we introduce context-aware semantic learning, where semantic labels are queried from full image context, enabling more accurate semantic prediction. Extensive experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detection performance while running over 500$\times$ faster than the previous state-of-the-art method.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

evidence.title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
evidence.abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

title: Quantum Graph Neural Networks: Architectures, Trainability, and Applications
abstract: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, with the aim of overcoming limits of classical graph neural networks in scalability, expressivity, and long-range information flow. Since the first Hamiltonian-based model in 2019, the field has produced many architectures, applications, and claims, but the evidence behind them has not been assessed systematically. This survey introduces a unified formalism that describes every QGNN as an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head, together with a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance and a resource model for comparing costs. We organize the literature into five architecture families (convolutional, equivariant, message-passing and recurrent, Hamiltonian, and hybrid) and compare them by qubit cost, symmetry, scalability, and evidence. We then review symmetry and geometric inductive biases (permutation, rotation, and Lorentz), the results on expressivity, trainability, noise, and scalability, and applications in high-energy physics, chemistry, finance, healthcare, earth observation, and transportation. An audit of datasets and evaluation practices leads to a minimum reporting protocol. Our main finding is that the design space is rich and symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, whereas the evidence remains thin: results are mostly simulated, on small graphs, at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has yet been established on tasks over classical graph data. We identify five open challenges and a research agenda covering provable advantage, equivariant and geometric designs, fault-tolerant implementations, and shared benchmarks. The coverage extends through 2026 and emphasizes recent work.

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.

title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.

title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
abstract: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE

title: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning
abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.

title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.

title: OmniScore-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Musical Score Reading
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.

title: Process Mining-Enabled Federated Anomaly Detection for the Industrial IoT
abstract: While federated anomaly detection enables the integration of local data insights across diverse nodes to reduce false positives, it inherently struggles with non-IID data. In practice, industrial IoT plants often operate under varying conditions and experience diverse environmental phenomena, resulting in significant heterogeneity in the monitored time series. In such settings, standard federated learning approaches fail to perform nuanced aggregation that accounts for these cross-node differences, ultimately leading to increased false positive rates. In this paper, we propose a process mining approach to evaluate the similarity of local node data against a reference provided by a global node. The global node utilizes these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation, producing personalized updates distributed across the network. We evaluate our approach using industrial IoT time-series data collected from manufacturing plants operating under distinct conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline achieves superior performance, yielding a 46.52% and 11.99% relative improvement in F1-score compared to isolated local training baselines and standard FedAvg, respectively, alongside a 51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation.

title: Speed-Variation Distillation for Generative Modeling
abstract: While diffusion models excel at image generation, their denoising trajectories pass through corrupted intermediate states far from the image manifold. We ask whether generation can instead proceed through recognizable images throughout the entire trajectory. We introduce a generative framework built around a variation-reducing degradation process that contracts diverse images toward a shared prototype while preserving recognizable intermediate states. Because such manifold traversal lacks a simple analytical form, we construct the trajectories using generative-prior-based image morphing. We then distill the reverse process into a diversification operator that transforms the prototype into increasingly varied samples. To resolve the one-to-many ambiguity of the reverse process, we associate each trajectory with its initial noise latent and apply perturbations to improve robustness against accumulated errors. At inference, every step yields a recognizable image, allowing early termination and enabling a controllable speed--variation trade-off.

Because such manifold traversal lacks a simple analytical form, we construct the trajectories using generative-prior-based image morphing. We then distill the reverse process into a diversification operator that transforms the prototype into increasingly varied samples. To resolve the one-to-many ambiguity of the reverse process, we associate each trajectory with its initial noise latent and apply perturbations to improve robustness against accumulated errors. At inference, every step yields a recognizable image, allowing early termination and enabling a controllable speed--variation trade-off.

title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
abstract: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.

title: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.

title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast.

title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.

title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
abstract: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

title: DoubleTake: Focused Verification of Visual Evidence for Long-Document Understanding
abstract: In long-document question answering, a vision-language model can answer incorrectly even when the retrieved pages contain sufficient evidence. Rereading those pages with the original question gives the model little guidance about which fact to check. We introduce DoubleTake, a training-free framework for focused verification of visual evidence. An initial reading produces a candidate answer and a separate evidence record that guides retrieval for a second reading. A planner compares the two candidates and their supporting evidence to formulate a factual question. A verifier answers it from the source images without seeing either candidate or evidence record, and a reasoner uses this observation to resolve the original question. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DoubleTake achieves the highest overall accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of four benchmarks. With the same pages and number of model calls, asking a focused factual question yields higher accuracy on all four benchmarks than asking the original question again. Our code is available at https://github.com/small-code-cat/double_take.
